source.title: Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet
source.authors: Ze-Yuan Hu; Akshay Subramaniam; Noel Keen; Tao Ge; Jaideep Pathak; Mohammad Shoaib Abbas; Suman V. Ravuri; K. Kashinath; N. Mahfouz; Peter M. Caldwell; Mike Pritchard; Noah D. Brenowitz

record.tranche_reason: The study runs a compute-scaling sweep for atmospheric AI emulation, a non-language-model setting, and reports test loss versus training FLOPs.
record.gate_note: The nine DiT configurations in Figure 3b report test loss against training FLOPs and are recorded separately. Results cited from prior work are not included. Rollout-fidelity results do not measure the scaling-law versions. The study does not fit or report power-law exponents.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own iso-FLOP sweep of 9 DiT configurations for km-scale atmospheric emulation and plots test loss against training FLOPs (Fig. 3b). That is a non-text setting bearing on V5. However, no power law is fitted and no values are tabulated, so the power-law form V5 names cannot be read from the results.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say loss 'decreases predictably with model FLOPs'. Smaller models are more compute-efficient at low budgets and larger models reach lower loss with more training, which they call consistent with Hoffmann et al. Patch size 1 is worse than 2 and 4 at equal FLOPs. Their headline scaling conclusion is that km-scale emulation needs about 10x more FLOPs per grid point than coarse AI weather models, due to higher entropy. No power law is fitted.
record.recipe_differences: This is an atmospheric emulation compute-scaling sweep, not a language-model pretraining scaling-law fit; it varies model tier and horizontal patch size and does not fit exponents or an optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss trend depends on model tier and horizontal patch size; the paper also reports width-versus-depth tradeoffs at fixed FLOPs, with the relative advantage changing between smaller and larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched forward FLOPs, horizontal patch size 1 gives higher test loss than patch sizes 2 and 4 (Fig. 3b), so tokenization matters beyond compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In patch-tokenized scientific emulators, loss at fixed compute depends on token granularity, not compute alone.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed FLOPs in an atmospheric emulator, wider beats deeper at small sizes; deeper has a marginal edge at large sizes (Fig. S14, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shape effects at fixed compute in non-LM transformers change sign with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Test loss is lowest at batch sizes up to 32; beyond that, training is unstable under linear LR scaling (Fig. S16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Critical batch size in km-scale atmospheric emulation.

fits_no_version.finding: Km-scale emulation needs about 10x more FLOPs per grid point than coarse weather models, attributed to higher data entropy (Table 1b, App. J).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute requirement scales with the information density of the data.

record.problems: The scaling-sweep loss values are shown only in a plot, with no numerical table or reported uncertainty. The study does not fit power laws, and tests only atmospheric emulation in this sweep.

untested.parts: Whether loss vs compute follows a power law (no fit, no exponent, no stated range of orders of magnitude). Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are also untested.

The text notes that smaller models are better at low budgets and larger ones at high budgets ('consistent with Hoffmann'). But no compute-optimal size or token allocation, and no exponent, is reported, and the setting is not language-model pretraining.
Width vs depth (Fig. S14) is studied in a weather emulator at fixed FLOPs, not in language models at fixed parameters.
Rollout stability is related to FLOP tier only qualitatively; there is no predictability analysis.
No exponents are fitted, so fit-dependence cannot be assessed.

missing.what: Width-vs-depth iso-FLOP test-loss sweep. It is not recorded and rows_left_out says 'None'.
missing.versions: none (bears on a V4-like question in a non-LM setting)

missing.what: Qualitative iso-FLOP crossover: smaller models are more compute-efficient at low budgets, larger ones reach lower loss with more compute. Only per-config figure rows exist.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is given. All linked rows are cannot_determine, because the study shows loss falling with compute but never establishes a power-law form. The reader's limits_scope label rested on an untested part (no fit), which per the rules belongs under untested. Other caveats: the sweep mixes schedules (three configs got extra cosine annealing, the rest constant LR), uses only 17 days of data, and the loss is Huber on normalized tendencies.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling in language models.
No small-run fit is used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation is reported.
The study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.

The study tests atmospheric emulation loss versus training compute, but does not fit a power law or test its exponents; it does not test other modalities or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer settings.
No downstream task performance is related to scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not assess fitting-method dependence, disagreement between published exponents, or departures from fitted power laws.
